name: Western Xia (Tangut Empire)
summary: An empire of the Tangut people in north-west China, with its own script, destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1227.

knownFor.label: Tangut script
knownFor.note: A complex script of about 6,000 characters.

location.value: Around the Hexi Corridor on the Silk Road; at its peak it ruled over 1,000,000 km² of north-central China, with its capital at Xingqing (now Yinchuan).

terrain.value: The irrigated Yellow River plain around today’s Yinchuan, the Helan Mountains, the Ordos and Gobi deserts, and the Hexi Corridor.

climate.value: Dry continental: hot summers, very cold winters and little rain outside the irrigated plain.

resources.value: Irrigated grain land, horses and camels, salt from desert lakes, and control of Silk Road oases.

disasters.value: Droughts and earthquakes; Mongol raids from 1205 brought famine.

urbanisation.value: The capital Xingqing (today’s Yinchuan) and oasis towns of the Hexi Corridor such as Liangzhou, Ganzhou and Dunhuang.

disease.value: Epidemics in sieges and famines, especially during the Mongol wars.

migration.value: Tangut clans moved from the Tibetan borderlands into the Ordos and Gansu before the state formed.

economicBase.value: Mainly agriculture, pastoralism and trade, especially with Central Asia; horse trade is mentioned. Salt is not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Controlled the Hexi Corridor section of the Silk Road; traded horses and salt with Song China for silk and tea.

wealth.value: Rich from trade tolls and from Song “gifts” of silk, silver and tea paid under the 1044 peace.

moneyAndTax.value: Bronze and iron coins with Tangut or Chinese writing; land taxes and payments from Song China.

inequality.value: Not well recorded; Tangut nobles ruled over Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur subjects.

governmentType.value: A monarchy: Jingzong built a Chinese-style central government with a Secretariat, a Bureau of Military Affairs and sixteen bureaus.

keyRulers.value: Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor in 1038 (Emperor Jingzong); Chongzong declared himself a Jin vassal in 1124; Xiangzong submitted to the Mongols in 1210; Emperor Mo surrendered in September 1227 and was executed. Renzong is not mentioned in the part of the page read.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Xi Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (1038 Li Yuanhao took the title of emperor; ten emperors in all; the last, Li Xian, ruled 1226–27)

succession.value: Hereditary in the Weiming (Li) family; regents and empress dowagers often held real power.

institutions.value: Chinese-style ministries, a written law code (the Tiansheng Code, about 1149–69) and state Buddhist offices.

stability.value: Lasted about 190 years despite wars with Song, Liao, Jin and finally the Mongols.

eliteConflict.value: Not well recorded; empress dowagers and court factions held power at times.

armyAndTech.value: Heavy armoured cavalry, camel-mounted catapults and mountain fortresses.

majorWars.value: A war with the Song in 1040–1044 and conflict with them until 1127; a failed Liao invasion in 1044; Mongol raids in 1205 and 1207 and an invasion in 1209; Genghis Khan attacked again in 1225 and the capital surrendered in September 1227, a month after his death.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Xi Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (1044 the Song agreed to annual payments (Qingli peace); Britannica describes a three-way truce with Song and Liao afterwards)

territoryChange.value: Held the Hexi Corridor and the Ordos region.

alliancesRivals.value: After a Liao invasion Jingzong made peace with the Song, who recognised him as ruler of Xia lands and agreed to annual tribute.

inventions.value: Some of the oldest surviving books printed with movable type are Tangut Buddhist texts from the 1100s.

scienceEducation.value: Translated the Buddhist canon into Tangut; Renzong set up schools and an imperial academy.

openness.value: Open to Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur influences.

communicationTransport.value: Horses and camel caravans across the desert; post stations along the Silk Road.

religion.value: The state religion blended Tibetan Tantric Buddhism with Chinese Mahayana Buddhism; Confucian and Taoist texts were also studied.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Xi Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Britannica: Buddhism was the state religion, unlike China; the museum page adds Han and Tibetan rites and Confucian ideas in law)

languageWriting.value: Tangut, written in its own script of about 6,000 characters, created in 1036.

artsArchitecture.value: Buddhist paintings and pagodas, the royal tombs at the foot of the Helan Mountains, and murals at Dunhuang.

socialStructure.value: Tangut nobility and warriors above Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur farmers, herders and merchants.

sharedIdentity.value: Tangut identity built on their own script, Buddhism and their emperors.

dailyLife.value: Rammed-earth houses in farming towns and felt tents among herders; millet, meat and dairy.

neighbours.value: Song China, the Liao and Jin dynasties, the Uyghur and Tibetan peoples, and the Mongols.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism as a state religion, mixing Chinese and Tibetan traditions.

riseSignals.value: The Tangut script was created in 1036 under Yeli Renrong; in 1038 Yuanhao declared himself emperor (Jingzong) with his capital at Xingqing, modern Yinchuan.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Xi Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (1038 founding and Xingqing (Yinchuan) as capital confirmed; the museum page says the script was ordered before the regime began)

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Renzong (1139–93), a time of peace, law-making and Buddhist learning.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (the museum page does not call Renzong’s reign a peak; it says troubles began after his death and gives his reign as 1140–1193 against Wikipedia’s 1139–93)

declineSignals.value: Mongol raids from 1205; Western Xia was destroyed by Genghis Khan’s army in 1227.

outcome.value: Annihilated by the Mongols in 1227; Emperor Mo surrendered in September 1227 and was executed. The museum page says Li Xian surrendered without a fight when Genghis Khan besieged Zhongxing (near Yinchuan) in early 1227; Wikipedia says the emperor was executed.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Western Xia (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Xi Xia; Hong Kong Heritage Museum: Xi Xia (checked 14 Nov 2026) (1227 conquest confirmed)

overallCertainty.value: Script long undeciphered; history partly known.
